Navigating the Crowded Gen4 SSD Market Upgrading your storage to a PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD is one of the most impactful improvements you can make to your system. However, the market is flooded with options, and not all Gen4 SSDs are created equal. Some are designed for maximum raw speed, requiring substantial cooling. Others prioritize power efficiency for laptops. Some are built specifically to meet the stringent requirements of the PlayStation 5. Choosing the wrong drive can lead to thermal throttling in a laptop, incompatibility with a console, or overpaying for performance you don’t need. You need a clear understanding of which drive matches your specific hardware and use case. Different Workloads Require Different Architectures The diversity in Gen4 SSDs stems from the varying demands of different devices and users. A desktop gaming PC has ample airflow and space for large heatsinks, allowing for maximum performance controllers. An ultrabook, conversely, has strict height limitations and relies on battery power, necessitating single-sided designs and power-efficient controllers. The PlayStation 5 requires specific sustained read speeds and has a defined physical space for heatsinks. FAQ Q1: Will a Gen4 SSD work in my older Gen3 motherboard? Yes. All addlink PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSDs are fully backward compatible with PCIe Gen3x4 platforms. However, the maximum speed will be limited by the Gen3 interface (typically capping around 3,500 MB/s). It’s still a great upgrade path, as you can carry the Gen4 drive forward to a new system later. Q2: Do I absolutely need a heatsink for a Gen4 SSD? For high-performance drives like the A95, A93, and S95 running in a desktop or PS5, a heatsink is highly recommended (and included with the A-series) to prevent thermal throttling under heavy loads. For laptops and ultrabooks using the S93, the drive is designed to operate efficiently without a bulky heatsink, relying on the laptop’s internal thermal management. Q3: What is HMB technology in the S90 Lite? Host Memory Buffer (HMB) technology allows DRAM-less SSDs like the S90 Lite to utilize a small portion of the computer’s system memory (RAM) to cache mapping tables. This significantly improves random read/write performance and responsiveness, allowing the drive to offer excellent performance at a lower cost compared to drives with dedicated onboard DRAM. Q4: Why does my 2TB drive show less capacity in Windows? This is normal for all storage devices. Storage manufacturers calculate capacity using the decimal system (1TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes). Windows operating systems calculate capacity using the binary system (1TB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes). Therefore, a 2TB drive will appear as approximately 1.86TB in Windows. Q5: Which drive is best for a thin laptop upgrade? The S93 is the definitive choice for thin laptops and ultrabooks. Its 2.25mm single-sided design ensures physical compatibility, and its power-efficient controller prevents excessive battery drain and heat generation in confined spaces. This utility allows you to monitor drive health, check SMART status, update firmware, and perform secure erases, helping you maintain your drive’s performance over its lifespan.
